questions.q: Per this lesson, what does naming a person as the cause of an incident actually teach the team?
options: It teaches people to under-report or hide details in the future, out of fear of being blamed
It teaches people to be permanently more careful with no downside
It has no effect on future behavior either way
It teaches junior staff to seek out more incidents to prove their skill
questions.explain: Blame doesn't make people more careful — it makes them better at hiding evidence, which is the opposite of what a postmortem needs.

questions.q: Why does this lesson call blamelessness a DevOps culture practice rather than just a documentation habit?
options: Because DevOps depends on people reporting problems fast and honestly, and blame culture punishes exactly that honesty
Because DevOps has no relationship to how postmortems are written
Because blameless language is required by SQL Server's terms of service
Because it only applies to database incidents and not application incidents
questions.explain: The lesson frames blamelessness as a precondition for the fast, honest feedback loops DevOps actually needs to function.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a blameless postmortem's anatomy, per this lesson?
options: Timeline, contributing factors, and action items
Blame assignment, punishment, and apology
Root cause, budget impact, and press release
Alert log, server specs, and vendor contact list
questions.explain: A timeline of facts, the conditions that made things worse or slower to detect, and specific owned fixes make up the structure.

questions.q: In the lesson's rewritten example, what does "the alert had no escalation path, so it went unacknowledged for 40 minutes" do differently than "the on-call DBA failed to notice the alert"?
options: It names a fixable system gap instead of ending the investigation at a person's failure to act
It removes the incident from the record entirely
It assigns blame to a different, more senior person instead
It changes the actual timeline of events described
questions.explain: Both sentences describe the same fact, but only the blameless version points at something an action item can actually close.

questions.q: What makes an action item in a blameless postmortem strong, according to this lesson's standard?
options: It is specific, owned, and would have prevented or caught the incident faster if it had already existed
It assigns responsibility to whichever team member was on call that night
It recommends a general reminder to "be more careful" going forward
It is left unassigned so no one feels singled out
questions.explain: The test for a good action item is whether it structurally changes something, not whether it feels reassuring to write.
